p: [interposing] Yes.

the majority of those are attorney lines. And so, but the— we have 13 vacancies currently, and those are a few attorney lines, but the bulk is non-attorney enforcement support. So, folks into our hotline to take reports of discrimination, folks for this newly-created role of civil rights case specialist who will help investigate discrim— claims of discrimination, and then a few folks throughout the agency for support.
And just a reminder, how many people are currently supporting the hotline?
There are currently eight people, and as part of the commissioner's restructure, we're moving more folks in there. So after we hire up fully, we should have a team of 15.
Okay. Between the Preliminary Budget hearing and today's hearing, have you hired any new employees? I'm sorry if you just said that.
We have, yes. Yeah, we've hired three new people since then.
Okay.
And then we have, I think, I believe four people pending OMB approval.

Okay. I know– and I know we've talked a lot about the attorney positions and that it's hard to recruit and retain folks. What are some of the actions that CCHR is taking to make those positions more attractive for prospective employees?

I will say that it has been in the past hard to recruit attorneys. It's not currently hard because attorneys who care about this are, like, fleeing the federal government and federal enforcement agencies. But it is hard to retain. That is, you know– our salaries can make other jobs more attractive. We intend to retain those attorneys by— in our restructuring, we've created more of a– different specialized roles that allow lawyers as they go through the lifetime of their career with us to take on more and more responsibility and get more and more litigation training. So the things that we offer that other

public interest jobs of the same salary band don't offer is a ton of trial experience, a ton of litigation experience, and that's really, you know, what we're trying to do, train people up, give them a lot of real-world experience, and get— and try to build in some pathways to advancement for them within the agency.
So when folks get a lot of litigation experience and training, but not the salary to go along with that, don't they most likely want to leave?
Depends on the person.

Okay. That's a nice answer. One of the available civil service titles you have is for an agency attorney intern, which has a minimum salary of just over $72,000. How many budgeted versus actual agency attorney interns does the Commission have?

So agency attorney intern is like a term of art for lawyers who are not yet admitted to the bar. When they get admitted to the bar, they do become Agency Attorney Ones, is my

understanding. So it's— I don't think it's a separate–

[interposing] Correct. So when you look at Agency Attorney Intern, it's at the bottom of a progression for agents or folks. So it's basically just how many attorney lines do we have funded? And I believe we are somewhere 20– I think about 20, I think 20 attorneys currently. So at any point, any of those folks could be an Agency Attorney Intern, Agency Attorney One, Two, or Three?
We don't hire Agency Attorney Interns that we don't intend to turn into Agency Attorneys once they pass the bar and get admitted.
And those folks actually—
[interposing] so there's a clear pathway for full-time?
Yes.
Yes.
Yes.
They are full-time actually. The intern— Agency Attorney Interns are full-time salaried, benefit employees.
Okay.
They just have two years to pass the bar and be admitted.
Understood.
And then they're at that point eligible to be an Agency Attorney One.
And is the hours and average caseload comparable to other fields?
Yeah, I think it's pretty comparable. So, the average attorney caseload is around 40. That's similar to Legal Aid Legal Services.

Okay, just a few more questions. Similar, talking about the attorneys, there are four levels of agency attorneys with minimum salaries ranging from $73,000 to 90— just over $96,000. What type of attorneys do you need the most? Which– and which ones impact caseload the most?

I wish there was a clean answer to this. People have differing opinions

about whether it's better to hire more mid-level people or just train up the people we have, but we do definitely have a need for more experienced litigators.
So more senior-level attorneys. And you said, how does this impact caseload?

I mean, not every attorney in our team does the same thing. Some people specialize more in complex investigations or complex, like, impact litigation, so there are different people who have different kinds of skill sets and specialty. But, you know, as a general rule, can more experienced attorneys take on more? Yes.

Okay, I'm going to talk about the Racial Equity Plan, and then I'll turn it back over to the Chair. So in April, they released the Preliminary Plan. The Commission submitted a plan which had short, medium, and long-term goals. The first goal aims to increase community outreach in the 33 Task Force on Racial Inclusion and Equity neighborhoods by the end of 2026. How many of the

neighborhoods is the Commission currently conducting outreach in?

Yeah, in fiscal year '26, we've conducted— we've conducted outreach in nearly all of them. Happy to give you back hard data points of which neighborhoods specifically we've been reaching out. But tree [sic] neighborhoods have been a priority for this agency for the past two years in outreach. And so, with that goal, it was really trying to concretize and communicate the work that we are already doing in those neighborhoods.
Okay, and so you'll let us know which ones you haven't targeted?
Yes.
Do you have a number, like, out of the 33, you think there's, like, six left or 10 left? You've covered two-thirds? 50 percent?

I can't give you an exact number right now, but I'm happy— I'm confident that we've done— more than the majority of neighborhoods have had direct outreach to them. And then separately, when there are— for those who don't

have direct outreach, we have connections to CBOs who are placed in those zip codes.
Okay. So in relationship to the decrease in budget, how are you planning to continue that outreach to those remaining neighborhoods?

Yeah, I think as the commissioner mentioned, we're really trying to build relationships and pathways with offices like the Mayor's Office for Mass Engagement, you know, the Commission on Gender Equity, all of the agencies that have specific outreach branches that can help us do this work and are close to the ground. And then separately, with our new created team of community partnerships, we're focusing on having strategic partnerships with movements and organizations in those neighborhoods. And the shift here specifically is where this agency wanted to be at the micro level of outreach. We need to be at the macro level of outreach, and we need to start working with folks who have trust from the community and don't have to go over that boundary of that trust in government. So folks who are undocumented are more likely to go to a

CBO that they trust. And so we need to be able to equip those CBOs with the tools and information they need to serve their community when they come in. So that's the bit of the shift in the strategy.
Okay, understood. And just in relationship to the first medium-term goal, expanding commission-initiated investigations– how many have you launched in 2026?

So our commission-initiated team is finally very recently fully staffed. And then we— so we initiate— there's like commission-initiated investigations and then commission-initiated complaints and then a whole universe of things in between. We have initiated a bunch of investigations. I don't— I'm not going to say off the top of my head because I don't know the answer, but I know that we've initiated quite a number of investigations into pay transparency, pay equity issues, as well as– I'm going to forget them. I think there's only one formal complaint, but when we initiate an investigation, there's really a number of purposes. One, it could turn into a complaint which turns into litigation, but we also do it as a

tool to work with community groups and organizers to help support their work and their goals. And so if we see what we think is a violation, we'll open up an investigation as part of a larger push to hold that landlord or that employer accountable. The goal is not always litigation. I mean, as any lawyer can tell you, the goal is almost never litigation. So we invest— we open up a lot of investigations, and I think it's our policy not to talk about them too much, but we've launched probably a dozen or so investigations this calendar year.
Okay.
And now that we have a fully staffed team, we will do more.
And how does— how many— what does a typical investigation require in terms of staff or personnel?

It totally depends on the complexity of the investigation. Some things, like, you know, like a huge landlord like Parkchester where we think that there's violations happening in like every unit in their portfolio, that's going to take an enormous amount of attorney time, both for

investigations and for litigation and for like enforcement post-litigation. And then other cases, you know, we're sending out requests for information, it may be only one or two lawyers. So it fully depends on the scope and the complexity. We intend to have more high-impact complex cases that affect larger numbers of people. Now that we have a dedicated team for that, that's sort of the whole goal of that team. And again, we intend to sort of work with grassroots organizations to determine what those strategic targets should be and to make sure that we're supporting their work and meeting them where they think we should be.
Okay, understood. I think last question on attorneys for a minute. How many are currently on the enforcement team?
I think we have 20 staff attorneys now. That's like frontline attorneys, and then we have, I think, six supervisors, and then senior management.
And what would be your— and did you say what your dream world number of attorneys would be?
I would never put an upper limit on that.
Or what did you request? What did you request for?
Over the three years, we requested for– I don't even know. I don't want to say, because I don't know.
I think– I don't have the exact number, but I can tell you 80 percent of our request was for enforcement staff.
That includes our—
[interposing] Yeah, that includes non-attorney–
enforcement staff, non-attorney?
Correct.
Okay.
Both. So it includes attorney and non-attorney.
Okay. Well, more than 20. You asked for more than 20, right?
Correct.

Right. Okay. I just have– my last line of questioning before I turn back to the Chair. There are some more that based on your testimony, but I'll come back to you after we open it up. This is on CORE’s feedback. I'm sure you all saw this, the score that CORE gave you all, it's 24. And for the record, that means it's, it has limited alignment with the racial equity rubric and has goals that lack specificity or measurable outcomes for community impact. So just curious, what's the plan to improve this score? And have you started any conversations?

Yeah, we're reaching out to CORE to better understand the score. I think one of the things that's— for us right now as we look at the score is there's no real rubric to measure where points are awarded, where points are taken off. And so once we have those conversations, we're happy to align those pieces. But again, those were goals that were set in place as part of the process where I think the Mayor's Office for Equity and Racial Justice and CORE both had opportunities to comment along the process. So we're— we've been in

communication with them, and we're happy to continue those conversations. But as of now, we don't really understand the score.
You take question with the rubric is what you're saying.
Just to understand it.

Okay. I'm just curious. Okay. So, you— they had specific goals for each agency, four for CCHR. I won't ask about every one of them, but the first one is to collaborate with relevant departments to create training programs for students in correctional facilities, dropouts, young adults, handicapped, or mentally disabled individuals. Do you all have the— one, the resources to implement this, and capacity to do it?
It's an interesting question because here's where— so I'm going to answer this from someone who used to work at the Department of Education.
I only ask interesting questions.

I know. We currently don't have a pedagogue on staff, right? So curriculum, we are doing everything we can, and part of the Commissioner’s restructuring is creating a team that is dedicated to education on civil rights. So moving folks into roles where their sole job is to think about how we educate New Yorkers, how we disseminate information. So, and as part of that work, there's capacity in there for specifically youth work. So we want to be growing all of our teams, right? But here's one of the things that I think I have been taking away from the Commissioner's reorg, that there are needs and there are wants. And while wants are negotiable, needs are not. And so we have to meet the need of New Yorkers.

I will say, in terms of trainings, one need that we have that we need to do internally before we're doing things like that is to make our trainings accessible. I don't know if you've taken one of our trainings recently, but, you know, an agency full of lawyers is going to lawyer, and we have to fix that. We have to be able to talk to people. And so we are doing– we're, like, doing a

360 about all of our communications. And I think for trainings, our goal is not that we are able to train everybody who needs to be trained. Our goal is to make trainings and partner with people so that those trainings can scale. Yeah.

No, I'm a huge believer in train-the-trainers model. I think that's— I think that's right. And I, as someone who's hosted many Know Your Rights trainings by lawyers, I'm always left translating what they're saying. Okay, last one on– I had a question on the third recommendation is again to provide pathways for youth to report discrimination complaints directly. Do you have– have you all considered what this would look like? And do you– again, do you have the capacity and resources to take that on?
We are definitely taking that one under advisement.
This one you, you agree with?
No, we're looking at, we're looking at it.
Oh, looking at.
There's like limits to, you know, minors filing complaints and stuff. So we're figuring out what we can do there and what the right approach is and what the right space is.
But we do want folks to know that anyone at any point can call and give an anonymous tip to the agency.
Also, anyone can call us, but in terms of outreach, we got to figure out what our, what our most effective lane is, I think there, especially for that one.
Okay.
Which I think is important.
Okay. I'll turn it back over to the Chair. Thank you.
Okay. So we're going to go with a few member questions starting with Deputy Speaker Williams.

Thank you. I have a whole bunch of questions, but the first thing I wanted to ask is– I was actually reviewing then-candidate Zohran Mamdani's Trump-proofing New

York City document, and in his document he said that he would fund CCHR $20 million— $21 million. Which is like significantly lower than what you have now. So I just wanted to say that I'm like slightly disappointed by that because I know that combating hate crimes and discrimination across the board was such a like pivotal component to his campaign. So, I just want to state that and I just want to say I feel like we went backwards because we have been fighting really hard the last couple of years and we've had some successes with allocations throughout the last couple of years. So I don't know how we're going backwards. I do hear the restructuring piece, and I don't know, maybe sometimes you have to take a few steps back to take 1,000 steps forward. Maybe that's what you all are doing. But it does kind of feel like we have moved backward with the funding. And then just on the Mayor's office of Mass Engagement, while I think that the intention of that off— that office is amazing. I'm just concerned about stability because when another administration comes on board, like, what if they don't have an Office of Mass Engagement? And then is that going to send CCHR

scrambling again in terms of your engagement? So I don't know if you have thought about, like, what sustainability looks like if you are relying more heavily on the Mayor's Office of Mass Engagement for outreach.

I will say in this, like, world of politics moving very fast, we think about sustainability of what we're doing all the time. It's one thing to change things when, when I'm in charge, and another thing if another administration comes in with different ideas. I think our agency is easily weaponized. So we do think about sustainability with what we're doing all the time and trying to make sure that we're not breaking something that works for us now and won't work in the future. So yes, we absolutely do think about that.

Okay. So I just wanted to turn back to some of the questions on the racial equity plan. I know the Chair asked a few of the questions. So one of the medium goals is to ensure current staff salaries meet New York City's true cost of living thresholds by the end of 2028. The true cost of living that was released alongside

the Prelim Racial Equity Plan states that the threshold for a single person with no dependents is $70,000 roughly. What percentage of staff currently meet this threshold?

Again, happy to get back to you with the exact percentage, but the— I think the majority of our staff is over $70K. The thing that makes the threshold itself very difficult to calculate on a staff-by-staff level is because includes the household income. And so we don't know how many of our staff are are married, are— have different variables. So what we want to do is focus on the salary, and we have very few staff who are on the lower end of that. So– and we've been working since drafting that goal to move the staff at the lowest end of salary up.

And I know there was some discussion on attorneys, and I know in previous hearings we've always discussed the attorney titles within CCHR, which sadly are a bit lower than the Law Department. So I just wanted to know if there has been any discussions around applying the similar Law Department titles to CCHR staff with OMB?

We have had conversations about what other titles could be available to us, and so we're hopeful that we can have more titles in our pocket, I guess. Okay. One of the strategies for this goal is to create a hiring committee to assess current hiring practices and operations. How would— who would be a part of this team, and would it be existing employees or specific staff for this purpose?

We already have a hiring committee, but we're also hiring a new Director of Mediations and EEO who will be leading that work along with all of our internal EEO work. So we're— but, you know, it'll include, like, our Deputy Commissioner of Enforcement and our Director of Operation— our Deputy Commissioner of operations, and probably Jose. So it's going to include people from all the verticals in our team to make sure that we're doing a good job of applying our own principles to our hiring process.

Jose can't do all of the things, even though I know he tries. That said, are current staffers going to be compensated

for the extra work, or it's just going to be like something else added to their portfolio?
The Director of Mediations and EEO, that's fully within their— the, the job description for their job.
Okay.
And then for folks who participate, their workload is adjusted to accommodate for it. So it's not, you know, what you–
[interposing] Additional.
Yeah.

Okay. One of your long-term goals is to improve accessibility at each of CCHR's five borough offices by the end of 2034, which will include the development of a rubric to gauge accessibility. How will the rubric be developed and who will be included in forming the rubric? And has CCHR begun to develop the rubric, and what is the deadline for the rubric to be created?

So as part of our Chief Savings Officer plan, and as well as part of our restructuring, we are trying to centralize more

people in the same office. Our bureau offices haven't been open to the public really on any kind of walk-in basis for a long time. And so we are trying to make ourselves— we're trying to come to people more often. We do mobile intake, we do intake at community groups and things like that, so we are trying to make sure that the offices that we do have open to the public are accessible and we are working on that, but I don't think it is our plan to have people coming to our five borough offices.

And I will just want to put a plug in, as, you know, the agency who enforces disability discrimination, we have a great team called Project Equal Access who is super versed in building accessibility and so we are very excited and lucky to be able to tap in their expertise to help us accomplish this goal.

Okay. Just something with CORE, and I know we've had this discussion before about increasing public availability of disaggregated data. So of the data that CCHR collects and reports on, how much and what

is currently disaggregated? And what steps will you take to ensure that all data is disaggregated?

So that is also communicating part of the need for a new case management system so that we can better run data reports. Right now, our limit to how we disaggregate information is based on either area of jurisdiction or protected category. And so we have no automated way right now to drill down into specifics of, uh, of particular protected categories. And we're hoping that with a new designed system, we will have that capacity to be able to quickly drill down to our data so that we can say— so when you say, Jose, I see— I'm making this number up— I see that 40 percent of your work is in gender discrimination. How does that actually translate? How much of it is discrimination against trans New Yorkers? How much of it is discrimination against women? It's so difficult to pull that data right now because it's manual. And so with the new system, we're hoping to be able to build into to it places where we can pull that type of data.

We are also very careful about what data we collect because we're the government and we don't have attorney/client privilege with the people who come to us. So we try to be extremely careful about what data we collect it and when we need to collect it and when we don't.
Yeah.

And then just like a follow-up question to some of the first round of questions that I had about the restructuring of CCHR’s engagement, which I do appreciate that approach, because as you know, I've had tons of questions about, like, CCHR's engagement. I know you have, like, a whole entire unit dedicated to community engagement. What type of, like, regular cadence of meetings and collaborations with other agencies do you plan to do? Like, I know, for instance, with DCWP, I remember having a lot of conversations about that inter-partnership, and I know that exists already, but as you think to build, I guess, similar partnerships with other agencies, what does that cadence look like?

Yeah, I— we absolutely want to build a relationship where we have regular standing meetings, whether that be monthly, quarterly, every other month. But then separately, what I think we're really hoping to do here is open the door to have ad hoc things happen and be able to meet more frequently and have relationships where communication just flows naturally. I think with Commissioner Clarke, we're seeing that with some of the agencies that we're already working with where the Commissioner to Commissioner communication is flowing really well. And so we just want to make sure that that trickles down to the staff level, so that our community partnerships team and our intergovernmental affairs team are communicating regularly with folks.

Yeah, like, when I think of source of income and, like, HRA as an example, like, I'm wondering, like, if a person is getting a voucher, like, do they also get, like, a one-pager that says if you have been discriminated against— does that level, like, micro level of coordination exist?

We're definitely building that across the different agencies, and I think as well as, you know, pick up the phone relationships to make sure that we can get people the things that they need. So for example, in source of income cases, we don't consider those cases closed until the person is fully leased up, and like the voucher is vouchering, and so we definitely make sure that we have the relationships we need to make that work for people.

And that's exact— that question is exactly the spirit of the strategy of the reorg is find people where the entry point actually is. So like working with corrections or people who are being– re-entering into society, do they know about fair chance housing, fair chance employment, those types of things, and catch them where they are, not where we want to find them.
Okay, thank you.

Okay, great. Just want to recognize we've been joined by Council Member Hanif on Zoom. And with that, we are going to go to

Council Member Hudson as well as— and then Council Member Wong.

Thank you so much, Chairs. And good morning. I just have a couple of questions, but I wanted to make one note about your testimony. If my math is correct, it appears as though you brought in— and maybe that's the wrong terminology, but saved perhaps or won $2.15 million, whether through restitution or damages or civil penalties. Plus you mentioned saving about $3 million in shelter costs. So first, thank you. Great job. The other thing though that I didn't hear mention of was that you've incurred an almost $2 million cut. And so I just wanted to note that on the record for an agency, a small agency, that is saving as much money as you are and winning damages and penalties and restitution in the amount of over $2 million, I think the loss of that funding is perhaps misplaced, I'll say. So I wanted to just ask a couple of questions about source of income discrimination which, as you know, is when a landlord refuses to rent to someone based on their income source, particularly when someone will pay with government assistance. Can you

share what percentage of your total complaints filed were related to source of income discrimination?
So I think we don't have the number on us, but I think it's— I'm going to— it's somewhere around a third, but we can get back to you with specific numbers.
Okay. And, how do you work with HRA to address source of income discrimination complaints clients attempting to use CityFHEPS vouchers?

I mean, I think, like I said, we sort of— most of our work is with the landlords to make sure that the landlords are doing the things that they need to do. We work with city— with HRA sort of the same way an advocate would, I think, through the various home-based providers and also, you know, contacting them directly when we need to to make sure that people get leased up. But primarily our enforcement is directed at the landlords and the brokers themselves.

There is one direct example for you, just concretely, of when folks have a voucher and they come to us but their

voucher is, like, about to expire. We can speak directly with folks to have— directly with HRA to have those vouchers extended. So that's one concrete way and one way that we track how we help folks obtain housing opportunities.

Thank you. And to date, how many source of income discrimination complaints have been filed by HRA clients attempting to use CityFHEPS vouchers in fiscal 2026, and can you compare that to the numbers in fiscal '25?

So we— I would say a healthy percentage of our source of income cases are not complaints that get filed. People call us and we intervene in our early intervention process. In those cases, it depends on what the situation is. If it's like with a broker, we may not even know what the kind of voucher is because it's sort of irrelevant in getting the broker to knock it off. So it definitely— like, we don't keep all of the data for everybody, and it depends, and I don't think we know off the top of our heads, but we can look at what we have and get back to you.

Okay. That would be great. And then I have just one last question, Chairs. Have you seen a change in the number of complaints related to source of income discrimination in fiscal '26 compared to fiscal '25?

Yeah, we're in the process of pulling together the numbers for fiscal '26, because what we do is— I'm sure the council knows this— we submit our annual report in September to the Council, which really aggregates all of our work across how many reports we've had, how many pre-complaint interventions we've done, how many complaints have been filed. And so we do that annually because, again, our case management system is hard to pull data from. So we're— at the end of June, we'll pull the entire year and then we'll run comparators to FY25. But I can just tell you that anecdotally, if you look at the past four years of our data, you can see the increase and you can see how housing is creeping up to be equal to employment discrimination.
Okay. And do you have any specific theories and what you believe to be the contributing factors?

I mean, I think it is, like, I— largely an issue of education, making sure that people know that it's illegal. I think part of what education does is it does give people, like, the power to stand up for themselves. We get a lot more complaints with people who have, like, videotaped their landlord and broker than we ever did before. That is incredibly effective. And so partially it's that. Partially it's the success of our precomplaint intervention team. They are very successful. Most people, we get them leased up within three or four weeks. That means that more advocates send us more clients, and so part of it is the success of our program, but I think— I don't want to pretend that it's not having to do with there being more source of income discrimination. I'm sure there is.
Great. Thank you both. Thank you, Chairs.
Thank you. Okay, Council Member Wong?

Thank you, Chairs. I don't have a sense, based on reading your testimony, like, how many cases you serve in a year and what is the breakdown? Like, how many are involved discrimination or antisemitism or that? Do you have that data?

Yeah, I'm happy to share with you our annual report for fiscal '25, and then when we publish 26’s, happy to share that with you as well. It will break down every report of discrimination we have received, including things that are— fail to state a claim for under the Human Rights Law. It will have data for everything that we have done early intervention for. It will have data for every complaint that we have filed. And it will have data on the closures of our cases, whether how many we have settled, how many we have done a probable cause determination, how many we've administratively closed, and the metrics of how many— how much damages we've secured for New Yorkers in that year, usually in the millions, and then how many

civil penalties for the City of New York, usually in the hundreds of thousands.

Yeah, okay, that takes me to my next question. Now, with the proposed $2 million budget cut in your commission, how are you gonna do your work if– like, anti-Semitic incidents, are up and so is discrimination complaints. How are you going to address that with this budget cut?
So, absolutely. Like I said, we fully have reorganized our agency to make sure that we're able to get more enforcement out of any amount that we have. And we do intend to do that.

Okay. I want to follow up on anti-Semitic complaints. 57 percent of reported hate crimes last year involve anti-Semitic incidents. What capacity does your agency have for Queens communities that are facing those incidents? Can you talk about it?

Absolutely. So I want to make clear that what we do– the Human Rights Commission, we do civil rights. So that's housing discrimination, employment discrimination, discrimination in public accommodations. We work very

closely with the NYPD to refer hate crimes, but we don't actually handle things that are violent crimes. And part of, I think, the benefit of our intake line, as well as our community partnerships, is making sure that everyone comes to us, gets the resources they need to go to the place that can help them out with whatever their issue is. We do take issues of discrimination, bias, hatred, bigotry towards the Jewish New Yorkers very, very seriously. And we do have– we do the— have both the capacity to enforce those cases, and we do a lot of outreach on those issues as well.
